record.original_question: Let A be an algebra and let S = End(A) be its endomorphism monoid. It is known that if S has commuting idempotents, then A has property RI, meaning the intersection of two retracts of A is also a retract; property UR, meaning each retract of A corresponds to a unique idempotent with that range; and the dual properties RI*, meaning the join of two coretracts of A is a coretract, and UR*, meaning each retraction has a unique section. Does the converse hold: do RI, UR, RI*, and UR* imply that the idempotents of End(A) commute?

evidence.quote: Let A be an algebra and S its monoid of endomorphisms.
It is known that if S has commuting idempotents then A has the properties:
(RI) the intersection of two retracts of A is also a retract,
(UR) to each retract of A corresponds a unique idempotent with that range,
and their duals. Is the converse true?
(RI*) the join of two coretracts of A is a coretract of A;
(UR*) each retraction h : A → R has a unique section (left inverse).

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ be a universal algebra and let $S = \mathrm{End}(A)$ denote its monoid of endomorphisms. A subalgebra $B \subseteq A$ is called a retract of $A$ if there exists an idempotent endomorphism $e \in S$ (i.e. $e^2 = e$) whose image is $B$; such an $e$ is called a retraction onto $B$, and an endomorphism $s \colon B \to A$ with $e \circ s = \mathrm{id}_B$ (viewed appropriately) is called a section of $e$. Dually, by a coretract one means the kernel congruence of a retraction, and the join of coretracts is the join in the congruence lattice. Consider the following four properties of $A$:
\begin{itemize}
  \item[(RI)] The intersection of any two retracts of $A$ is again a retract of $A$.
  \item[(UR)] To each retract of $A$ there corresponds a unique idempotent of $S$ whose image equals that retract.
  \item[(RI*)] The join of any two coretracts of $A$ is again a coretract of $A$.
  \item[(UR*)] Each retraction in $S$ has a unique section.
\end{itemize}
It is known that if the idempotents of $S$ commute (i.e. $ef = fe$ for all idempotent $e, f \in S$), then $A$ satisfies (RI), (UR), (RI*), and (UR*).

Question: Does the converse hold? That is, if an algebra $A$ satisfies all four properties (RI), (UR), (RI*), and (UR*), must the idempotents of $\mathrm{End}(A)$ commute?
artifact.status_search_result: The converse problem (originally posed by FitzGerald) has been resolved in the negative: an algebra satisfying all four properties (RI), (UR), (RI*), (UR*) whose endomorphism monoid nevertheless contains non-commuting idempotents has been constructed, in work by Hemelaer and Rogers published in Semigroup Forum (2021).

status_evidence.title: Solution to a problem of FitzGerald
status_evidence.snippet: FitzGerald identified four conditions (RI), (UR), (RI*), (UR*) necessarily satisfied by an algebra whose endomorphism monoid has commuting idempotents and asked whether these are sufficient. We give an example showing they are not.
status_evidence.claim: The converse implication is false: an explicit algebra satisfies the four properties but End(A) does not have commuting idempotents.

status_evidence.title: Solution to a problem by FitzGerald (arXiv:2011.12129)
status_evidence.snippet: An example of an algebra satisfying the four properties is given such that its monoid of endomorphisms does not have commuting idempotents.
status_evidence.claim: A counterexample to the converse has been constructed.
